Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

We represent: defendant insurer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an insurer has no duty to defend where the complaint's allegations fall entirely within a policy exclusion.

Cite at least six decisions of the First Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. BECAUSE EVERY ALLEGATION IN THE COMPLAINT FALLS WITHIN THE [__________] EXCLUSION, THE INSURER OWED NO DUTY TO DEFEND.

#### A. The duty to defend is measured by comparing the complaint to the policy.

Under the law governing this dispute, an insurer's duty to defend turns on the allegations of the underlying complaint read against the terms of the policy. This Court has repeatedly applied that comparison. *See Open Software Found., Inc. v. U.S. Fid. & Guar. Co.*, 307 F.3d 11, 14 (1st Cir. 2002); *Liberty Mut. Ins. Co. v. Metro. Life Ins. Co.*, 260 F.3d 54, 61 (1st Cir. 2001); *OneBeacon Am. Ins. Co. v. Commercial Union Assurance Co. of Can.*, 684 F.3d 237, 241 (1st Cir. 2012). The duty arises only when the complaint's allegations are "reasonably susceptible" of an interpretation that states a claim covered by the policy. *See Open Software*, 307 F.3d at 14; *Euchner-USA, Inc. v. Hartford Cas. Ins. Co.*, 754 F.3d 136, 140 (1st Cir. 2014). The inquiry is objective. The court asks what facts the complaint pleads, not what legal labels the plaintiff attaches or what the insured hopes to prove. *See Liberty Mut.*, 260 F.3d at 61.

The duty to defend is broader than the duty to indemnify, but it is not boundless. An insurer need not defend when the underlying complaint, fairly read, alleges only conduct the policy excludes. *See Vt. Mut. Ins. Co. v. Zamsky*, 732 F.3d 37, 41 (1st Cir. 2013); *Nautilus Ins. Co. v. Jabar*, 188 F.3d 27, 29 (1st Cir. 1999).

#### B. Exclusions are enforced as written once the insurer shows they apply.

The insurer bears the burden of establishing that an exclusion applies. Once it does so, the court enforces the exclusion according to its plain terms. This Court has consistently refused to rewrite unambiguous policy language to create coverage the parties did not bargain for. *See Peerless Ins. Co. v. Brennon*, 564 F.3d 1, 4–5 (1st Cir. 2009); *Euchner-USA*, 754 F.3d at 140–41; *Nautilus*, 188 F.3d at 29–30. Where the exclusion is clear, the court will not stretch the "reasonably susceptible" standard to find a possibility of coverage the pleaded facts do not support. *See Zamsky*, 732 F.3d at 41–42.

#### C. The Complaint pleads only excluded conduct.

The [__________] Exclusion removes from coverage [quote operative exclusionary language]. The underlying Complaint alleges that [summarize factual allegations, with citations to the Complaint]. Each count rests on that same conduct. Counts [__] through [__], whether styled as [negligence / breach of contract / other], derive from the same excluded facts and seek recovery for the same excluded injury.

Because the exclusion turns on the nature of the conduct alleged, the labels on the counts do not matter. This Court looks to the facts pleaded, not the theory of liability. *See Liberty Mut.*, 260 F.3d at 61; *OneBeacon*, 684 F.3d at 241–42. A plaintiff cannot trigger a defense obligation by pleading in the alternative a legal theory that depends on the same excluded facts. Nor can an insured rely on speculation that the plaintiff might later amend or prove something different. The duty to defend is determined by what the Complaint actually alleges. *See Open Software*, 307 F.3d at 14–15; *Peerless*, 564 F.3d at 5.

#### D. No allegation is even potentially outside the exclusion.

Defendant does not dispute that doubts about whether a complaint states a covered claim are resolved in favor of the insured. But that principle has no application here. The Complaint contains no allegation that, read generously, describes covered loss. It does not allege [identify the missing facts that would take the claim outside the exclusion]. Absent such allegations, there is no "possibility" of coverage to resolve in the insured's favor. *See Euchner-USA*, 754 F.3d at 141; *Zamsky*, 732 F.3d at 42.

The insured's contrary position depends on facts outside the Complaint, or on a strained reading of the exclusion that would render it meaningless. Neither supports a duty to defend. *See Nautilus*, 188 F.3d at 30.

#### E. Conclusion

Because the Complaint alleges only conduct falling squarely within the [__________] Exclusion, no claim was even potentially covered, and Defendant owed no duty to defend. The district court's judgment should be affirmed.
